The Markov property and a noisy grid world

intro.why: The MDP is the mathematical language of all of RL. Dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, TD, DQN and policy gradients are all ways of solving (approximately) the Bellman equations introduced here.

symbols: probability of next state s′ and reward r given s, a
return: discounted sum of future rewards
state- and action-value functions under π

sections.title: The agent–environment interface and the MDP
sections.plain: A precise model of the loop: states, actions, how the world responds, and rewards.
sections.body:
A finite Markov decision process is defined by finite sets of states $\mathcal S$, actions $\mathcal A(s)$ and rewards $\mathcal R \subset \mathbb R$, together with the dynamics

$$p(s',r\mid s,a) \doteq \Pr\{S_t=s', R_t=r \mid S_{t-1}=s, A_{t-1}=a\},\qquad \sum_{s'}\sum_{r} p(s',r\mid s,a) = 1$$

From $p$ we can derive everything else, e.g. state-transition probabilities $p(s'\mid s,a) = \sum_r p(s',r\mid s,a)$ and expected rewards $r(s,a) = \sum_r r\sum_{s'}p(s',r\mid s,a)$ or $r(s,a,s')$. An MDP is often summarised as $(\mathcal S, \mathcal A, p, r, \gamma)$ plus a start-state distribution and, for episodic tasks, terminal states.

The framework is abstract and flexible: time steps need not be fixed intervals, actions can be low-level torques or high-level decisions, and states can be sensor readings or symbolic descriptions.

sections.title: The Markov property and grid-world dynamics
sections.plain: The present state contains everything about the past that matters for the future.
sections.body:
Markov property: the probability of each possible $S_t, R_t$ depends only on the immediately preceding state and action, not on earlier history:

$$\Pr\{S_{t+1}, R_{t+1}\mid S_t, A_t\} = \Pr\{S_{t+1}, R_{t+1}\mid S_0, A_0, R_1, \dots, S_t, A_t\}$$

It is a restriction on the state, not on the decision process: the state must summarise all relevant past information (e.g. a chess position, or velocity as well as position for a moving robot).

Grid world. The agent moves on a grid with walls. The intended move succeeds 80% of the time; 10% it slips left and 10% right (relative to the intended direction); bumping a wall means staying put. Each step costs a small living reward (e.g. −0.04, battery drain); special cells give +1 or −1 and end the episode. Because "North" does not reliably go north, a fixed plan is not enough: the agent needs a policy and must reason with expectations over next states.

sections.title: Rewards, goals and the reward hypothesis
sections.plain: Everything we want can be phrased as maximising expected total reward, so reward what you want, not how.
sections.body:
Reward hypothesis. All of what we mean by goals and purposes can be thought of as the maximisation of the expected value of the cumulative sum of a received scalar signal (reward).

The reward signal tells the agent what to achieve, not how. Prior knowledge about how to do it belongs in the initial policy or value function, not in the reward.

  • Chess rewarded per captured piece: the agent may sacrifice the game to grab material.
  • A vacuum rewarded per unit of dirt collected: it may dump dirt and collect it again.
  • Maze: −1 per step until escape makes the agent escape quickly.

Mis-specified rewards lead to reward hacking (M14): the agent optimises exactly what was written, not what was meant.

sections.title: Episodic and continuing tasks; returns and discounting
sections.plain: The return is the (discounted) total of future rewards; it must stay finite.
sections.body:
Episodic tasks break into episodes ending in a terminal state at time $T$; continuing tasks go on forever. The agent maximises the expected return:

$$G_t \doteq R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k R_{t+k+1},\qquad G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\,G_{t+1}$$

$\gamma = 0$ is myopic; $\gamma \to 1$ is far-sighted. With $\gamma<1$ and bounded rewards the sum is finite. Episodic and continuing tasks are unified by treating the terminal state as absorbing with reward 0 (and allowing $\gamma = 1$ only when episodes end).

Worked returns ($\gamma = 0.5$): rewards $[1,2,3]$ give $G = 1 + 0.5\cdot2 + 0.25\cdot3 = 2.75$; the reversed $[3,2,1]$ give $3 + 1 + 0.25 = 4.25$ (earlier rewards count more). Reward +1 forever with $\gamma = 0.9$: $G = \sum_k 0.9^k = 1/(1-0.9) = 10$.

Adding a constant. In a continuing discounted task, adding $c$ to every reward adds $c/(1-\gamma)$ to every return, so the optimal policy is unchanged. In an episodic task the added amount depends on episode length, so it can change the optimal policy (a positive constant rewards dragging episodes out; a negative one rewards ending them quickly). Code example ex2 shows exactly this in grid world.

sections.title: Policies and value functions
sections.plain: How good is a state (or a state–action pair) if I follow this policy from here?
sections.body:
A policy $\pi(a\mid s)$ gives action probabilities in each state. Its value functions:

$$v_\pi(s) \doteq \mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s],\qquad q_\pi(s,a) \doteq \mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s, A_t=a]$$

They are related by

$$v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\, q_\pi(s,a),\qquad q_\pi(s,a) = \sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\big[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')\big]$$

$v_\pi$ averages over the policy's choices; $q_\pi$ fixes the first action and then follows $\pi$. Value functions can be estimated from experience: averaging observed returns (Monte Carlo, M6) or bootstrapping (TD, M8).

sections.title: The Bellman expectation equation
sections.plain: A state's value equals the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of where you land.
sections.body:
Using $G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}$:

$$v_\pi(s) = \sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\big[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')\big]\quad\text{for all } s$$

This expresses a consistency between a state's value and its successors' values; $v_\pi$ is its unique solution (a linear system of $|\mathcal S|$ equations). Backup diagrams draw it as: state → (policy branches) actions → (dynamics branches) next states.

Worked backup. Random policy (0.25 per action), $\gamma = 0.9$, deterministic moves with reward 0, neighbours valued 2.3, 0.7, −0.4, 0.4. Targets $0.9\,v(s')$ = 2.07, 0.63, −0.36, 0.36; $v(s) = 0.25 \times 2.70 = 0.675$.

Code example ex1 solves the linear system exactly for the noisy grid world under the random policy and checks that one backup reproduces each value.

sections.title: Optimal policies and the Bellman optimality equation
sections.plain: The best policy is greedy with respect to the optimal values, which satisfy a max-version of Bellman.
sections.body:
Policies are partially ordered: $\pi \ge \pi'$ iff $v_\pi(s) \ge v_{\pi'}(s)$ for all $s$. There is always at least one optimal policy $\pi_*$, and all optimal policies share

$$v_*(s) \doteq \max_\pi v_\pi(s),\qquad q_*(s,a) \doteq \max_\pi q_\pi(s,a) = \mathbb E[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_*(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s,A_t=a]$$

Bellman optimality equations: the value of a state under an optimal policy equals the expected return of the best action from it:

$$v_*(s) = \max_a\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\big[r+\gamma v_*(s')\big],\qquad q_*(s,a) = \sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\big[r+\gamma\max_{a'}q_*(s',a')\big]$$

These are nonlinear (because of max). Given $v_*$, any policy greedy with respect to it (one-step lookahead) is optimal; given $q_*$, no lookahead is needed: $\pi_*(s) = \arg\max_a q_*(s,a)$. Solving them exactly needs the model, enough computation and the Markov property, conditions rarely met, so most RL methods solve them approximately.

Grid world (ex2, $\gamma = 1$): living reward −0.04 gives values 0.81, 0.87, 0.92 along the top row and a policy that takes the long safe route; −0.4 takes the shorter path past the −1; −2.0 rushes to the nearest exit even if it is −1; a positive living reward (+0.5, $\gamma = 0.9$) makes the agent avoid both exits.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Partial observability. If the agent's observation is not Markov (e.g. a single video frame lacks velocity), stack recent observations or use memory (RNNs); formally this is a POMDP.
  • Discounting as uncertainty. γ can be read as a probability 1 − γ that the process terminates at each step, or as preferring sooner rewards.
  • Reward is part of the environment, even when computed inside a robot: the agent must not be able to change it arbitrarily, or it will.
  • Linear system cost. Solving v = r + γPv directly costs O(|S|³), which is why iterative DP (M4) is preferred for large state spaces.

code.explain: Computes the worked returns (2.75, 4.25, 10), builds the 3×4 noisy grid world's transition matrix under the random policy, solves (I − γP)v = r exactly, and checks one state with a single Bellman backup; then the 0.675 worked backup.
